title: Hop Test Cluster by Gustavsson | ACL Return to Play Testing
purpose: Gustavsson's three-hop battery to compare single-leg hop performance (and performance under fatigue) between injured and uninjured sides after ACL injury/reconstruction, for rehab progression and return-to-sport decisions.
structure: Lower-limb power, control and endurance after ACL injury; scored with the limb symmetry index (LSI = involved / uninvolved × 100).
procedure: 1) Vertical jump: countermovement jump, hands behind the back, flight time converted to height (contact mat, or the MyJump2 app validated by Haynes et al. 2019). 2) Hop for distance: single-leg hop landing on the same leg, hands behind the back, controlled balanced landing with the foot kept in place; distance from toe at push-off to heel at landing. 3) Side hop: hop sideways between two tape strips 40 cm apart for 30 s, hands behind the back; count successful hops, touching the tape is an error, >25% errors → second 30 s trial after 3 min rest.
positive: LSI > 90% is generally classified as normal; one or more tests with abnormal LSI classifies the patient as abnormal.

accuracy.source: Gustavsson et al. 2006: test-retest ICC 0.85-0.97; battery identified healthy subjects with 84% accuracy (3 normal LSIs) and classified patients as abnormal with 88% accuracy (≥1 abnormal LSI) at 6 and 11 months post-reconstruction

notes: Page rates high clinical value. LSI can overestimate knee function: ACL-reconstructed athletes show bilateral deficits versus normative data (Gokeler et al. 2017; Wellsandt et al. 2017), so pre-injury data or norms by age/sex/sport are preferable. Test also in a fatigued state: of patients with LSI > 90%, only 32% kept ≥ 90% when fatigued (Augustsson 2004; page text says 2014). Only one part of return-to-sport clearance.

title: Drop Jump Test | Dynamic Knee Valgus | Post ACL Surgery Test
purpose: Observe dynamic knee valgus on landing to classify a low- or high-risk landing mechanism for non-contact ACL injury (deficient hip neuromuscular control).
structure: Frontal-plane knee alignment (patella relative to the first toe) during a drop-landing and vertical jump; trunk and hip control.
procedure: Patient stands on a 31 cm box, drops to the floor and immediately performs a maximal vertical jump with the arms in the 'stop position' (shoulders 45° abducted, elbows 90° flexed). 3 practice trials, then 9 consecutive trials with 10 s rest. Film and review in slow motion (e.g. Hudl app).
positive: High-risk landing: the patella moves inward and ends medial to the first toe. Low-risk: patella stays in line with the first toe.

accuracy.source: Ekegren et al. 2009 observational risk screening (intra-/inter-rater kappa 0.75-0.85); values judged inadequate

notes: Add other tests for high-risk characteristics; how much valgus predisposes to injury is unknown, so screening validity is unclear (Krosshaug et al. 2016: poor screening test in 710 female athletes). Unilateral knee valgus with ipsilateral trunk motion may matter; single-leg drop jumps show greater alignment change than bilateral, so unilateral hop tests are also useful. Page writes the app name as 'Huddle'.

title: Star Excursion Balance Test | Postural Control | Return to Play
purpose: Dynamic postural-control test with single-leg reaches in eight directions (SEBT); differentiates chronic ankle instability, patellofemoral pain and ACL reconstruction and helps identify injury risk.
structure: Lower-limb dynamic balance; reach distance normalized to leg length.
procedure: Six tape strips at 45° form an 8-direction star. 4-6 practice trials per direction, then 5 min rest. Barefoot single-leg stance, hands on hips, reach as far as possible along each tape, touching lightly with the most distal part of the reaching foot without weight transfer; the examiner marks the farthest point. Trials are void if the touch is heavy, the foot rests, ground contact is needed for balance, or the stance foot lifts/shifts. Return to the centre between reaches; 3 full circuits per leg. Score: mean of 3 trials per direction (16 values), each divided by leg length × 100; compare sides.
positive: Asymmetry or low composite score. Examples on the page: anterior reach asymmetry > 4 cm predicted higher lower-limb injury risk in basketball players (Plisky et al. 2006); composite < 90% in collegiate American football players = 3.5× injury likelihood (page attributes this to Pollock et al. 2010; reference list has Butler et al. 2013).

accuracy.source: Reliability only: Gribble et al. 2013, inter-rater 0.86-0.92

notes: Page rates high clinical value. Performance and injury risk vary hugely between sports and sexes, so generalize cut-offs with care. Shortened version: Y-Balance test.

title: Y-Balance Test | Postural Control | Return to Play (RTP) Testing
purpose: Shortened Star Excursion Balance Test using the anterior, posteromedial and posterolateral reaches to find deficits and asymmetries and support return-to-play decisions.
structure: Lower-limb dynamic balance; reach distance normalized to leg length.
procedure: Three tape strips in a Y (135° between anterior and each posterior strip, 45° between the posterior strips). 4-6 practice trials per direction; 3 recorded trials. Anterior reach: toes of the stance foot at the zero mark; posterior reaches: heel at the zero mark. Barefoot, hands on hips, reach as far as possible touching the tape lightly with the toes; 3 trials right stance then 3 left, per direction. Void if heavy touch, resting at the midpoint, ground contact for balance or stance-foot shift. Score: mean of 3 trials per direction (6 values) divided by leg length × 100.
positive: Asymmetry or low composite score. Page examples: composite < 98.6% in college football players = 3.5× injury risk (Butler et al. 2013); anterior reach asymmetry > 4 cm predicted injury in basketball players (Plisky et al. 2006). No clear cut-offs because of variance between sports and sexes.

accuracy.source: Reliability only: page states 'excellent inter-rater reliability between 0.48-0.78' attributed to Plisky et al. 2006 (reference list gives Plisky 2009)

notes: SOURCE NOTE: calling 0.48-0.78 'excellent' is inconsistent with usual reliability thresholds; recorded as written. Related: SEBT, drop jump, hop test cluster.

title: ACL Rehab Phase 1 | Anterior Cruciate Ligament Post-Op Exercises
purpose: First phase of rehabilitation after ACL reconstruction: regain normal joint function (reduce swelling, full extension, normal patellofemoral motion, selective quadriceps control, normal gait).
structure: ACL graft (bone-patellar tendon-bone or hamstring), patellofemoral joint, quadriceps; the ACL also has a neuromuscular role (about 2.5% mechanoreceptors, which do not regrow after injury).
procedure: Mobility: heel slides, knee extension with a towel under the knee, manual mobilization of extension or the patellofemoral joint if needed; crutches until gait is symmetrical; ergometer cycling for warm-up/mobilization. Strength: isometric, concentric and eccentric closed-chain exercises allowed early; squats/leg press safest within 0-60° flexion in the first 3-4 weeks. Open-chain knee extension only after 4 weeks within 90-45°, adding about 10° extension per week (90-35° at 5 weeks, 90-25° at 6 weeks); external resistance after 4 weeks with a patellar tendon graft but only after 12 weeks with a hamstring graft. Straight leg raises and side-lying abduction do not strain the ACL and can start in week 1. Start neuromuscular/balance training early.
notes: References include Escamilla 2012, Dutch guideline (Meuffels 2012), van Grinsven 2010, van Melick 2016, Risberg 2007, Wright 2008. The page text contains leftover production notes ('In een table naast Kirsten', 'show pendulum on the bike').

title: ITB Syndrome Rehab | Evidence-based Iliotibial Band Exercises
purpose: Five-stage rehabilitation programme for iliotibial band syndrome in runners (after Tom Goom), built on the three components of Willy & Meira 2016: peak loads, energy storage and release, cumulative load.
structure: Iliotibial band, probably a compression injury; behaves like a tendon storing and releasing energy (Eng et al. 2015), so stiffness is desirable (Friede et al. 2020: physiotherapy improved outcomes and increased ITB stiffness by 14%). Stretching and foam rolling are not useful and may worsen compression.
procedure: Stage 1 (pain-dominant, pain on stairs/fast walking): stop running, especially trail/downhill; fast treadmill walking at 8-10° incline, or cycling with a low saddle/swimming; low-load hip abductor/extensor work: clam shells, side-lying abduction, Thomas/ITB excursion exercise 10×10 s. Enter the load-dominant phase when stairs are pain-free. Stage 2 (heavy slow resistance, 3×/week until return to running): side planks, single-leg bridges, fire hydrants, split squats (trailing leg trained), side lunges against a band; 3×10-12 progressing to 4×6-8 near failure. Stage 3 (plyometrics, about 1 week): mini squat jumps, reverse lunge + hop, lateral skaters, tempo run with bands; advanced: split jumps, squat jump to single-leg landing, single-leg hops. Stage 4: graded return to level running (couch-to-5K plan), lower incline from 8-10° to 5° to level, mirror gait retraining: wider step width, bigger knee window, 5-10% higher cadence; cues individualized. Stage 5: gradually add downhill and trail running on separate days, then combined.
notes: Willy et al. 2012: glute strengthening does not change running mechanics, mirror gait retraining does. Input credited to Rich Willy, Tom Goom and Benoy Mathew.

title: Best Hamstring Exercises | Hamstring Injury Rehab
purpose: Choose hamstring exercises by region-specific muscle use (MRI study, Mendez-Villanueva et al. 2016) for late-stage rehab and injury prevention.
structure: Four hamstring bellies: semimembranosus, semitendinosus, long and short head of biceps femoris.
procedure: Flywheel leg curl and, to a lesser extent, the Nordic hamstring curl target the short head of biceps femoris (and semitendinosus/semimembranosus); the hip-extension conic pulley selectively loads the proximal long head of biceps femoris; the Russian belt exercise is an add-on. Four exercises demonstrated in the video.
notes: For an acute hamstring injury the page recommends the Askling protocol first. See also Nordic hamstring curl variations.

title: Nordic Hamstring Curl Variations | Hamstring Injury Rehab
purpose: Partner-free variations of the Nordic hamstring curl for hamstring strain prevention/rehab, also useful to build up gradually to the full exercise.
structure: Hamstrings; the Nordic curl mainly works the short head of biceps femoris and semitendinosus (Mendez-Villanueva et al. 2016).
procedure: Variations shown: pulldown machine, resistance bands, Swiss-ball roll-out.
notes: To cover semimembranosus and the long head of biceps femoris as well, see the best hamstring exercises page; for an acute injury use the Askling protocol. Page text contains leftover production notes ('plaque research', 'show clip').

title: Askling Protocol | Hamstring Strain Rehabilitation
purpose: Early rehabilitation protocol for acute hamstring strains emphasizing loading during lengthening (Askling et al. 2013 RCT in Swedish elite football, superior to conventional protocols).
structure: Hamstrings: biceps femoris (long and short head), semitendinosus, semimembranosus. Stretching-type injuries (glide tackle, high kick) mostly affect semimembranosus; sprinting-type injuries affect the long head of biceps femoris.
procedure: 1) The Extender: stabilize the thigh with the hip at about 90°, slow knee extensions to just before pain; 3×12, twice daily. 2) The Diver: stance leg slightly flexed, swing leg knee 90°, dive forward by flexing the hip with arms extended forward; start slow, increase speed; 3×6 every other day. 3) The Glider: upright trunk, one hand on support, legs slightly split, weight on the heel of the injured leg with 10-20° knee flexion, glide backward on the other leg and stop before pain; return using the arms, not the injured leg; progress distance and speed; 3×4 every third day.
notes: Progress later to exercises covering all hamstring heads (best hamstring exercises page).
